caption: Figure 1. UML notation (see ISO TS 19103, Geographic information - Conceptual schema language)
shows: Legend of the UML diagram notation (draw.io SVG, text inside foreignObject). Left column: a role label on an association line from Class #1 to Class #2 (filled arrowhead = navigable association). Multiplicity examples next to 'Class' boxes: no label = 'Only one', '0...*' = 'Zero or more', '0...1' = 'Optional (zero or one)', '1.. *' = 'One or more', 'n' = 'Specific number'. Right column: 'Aggregate class' joined to Class #1..#n ('Aggregation between classes', hollow diamond at the aggregate end) and 'Superclass' with Subclass #1..#n ('Class inheritance (subtyping of classes)'). Labels contain typos ('0...*', 'Associtation').
lesson: Every association end in the later UML diagrams carries a multiplicity; an unlabelled end means exactly one. The role name sits at the target end and equals the XML child element name. Inheritance means the subclass carries everything of the superclass (e.g. everything derived from _OpenDriveElement may carry g_additionalData).
right: Treat an unlabelled association end as exactly 1 (mandatory, single)
Map role names (e.g. +geometry, +lane) directly to XML child element names
Treat '1..*' as 'at least one must be written'
wrong: Reading '0...*' (three dots, a drawing typo) as something other than '0..*'
Assuming an unlabelled end means optional - it means exactly one, so omitting that child produces invalid output
Treating aggregation as reference-by-ID - in OpenDRIVE XML aggregation becomes nested child elements

caption: Figure 2. UML attribute notation
shows: UML class t_header (abstract parent _OpenDriveElement in italics). All attributes public '+': revMajor: integer and revMinor: integer with no multiplicity; name: string [0..1], version: t_header_Version [0..1], date: string [0..1], north/south/east/west: double [0..1], vendor: string [0..1]. revMinor is boxed red 'mandatory attribute'; name boxed cyan 'optional attribute'.
lesson: An attribute without a [0..1] suffix is mandatory and must always be emitted; [0..1] attributes may be omitted entirely. For the header only revMajor and revMinor are required; the bounding box north/south/east/west is optional.
right: Always write <header revMajor="1" revMinor="7">
Omit optional attributes when no value is known instead of writing empty or zero placeholders
Write north/south/east/west only when computed from the real geometry bounds
wrong: Writing name="" or date="" as fillers (an empty string is a value, not absence)
Writing north=0 south=0 east=0 west=0 as defaults - asserts a wrong bounding box
Omitting revMinor because 'version' was written - version is a separate optional attribute

section: 3.1 Positioning of ASAM OpenDRIVE within ASAM activities
caption: Figure 3. Relation between ASAM OpenDRIVE, ASAM OpenCRG, and ASAM OpenSCENARIO
shows: Three product tiles: OpenDRIVE = 'Static Road Network Description' (intersection with lane arrows and traffic lights, no vehicles); plus OpenSCENARIO = 'Dynamic Scenario Description' (same intersection with vehicles and coloured trajectories) equals 'Scenario description, with dynamic and static content'. A curved arrow leads from the OpenDRIVE tile down to OpenCRG = 'Static Road Surface Description' (cobblestones, pothole, lane-marking close-up).
lesson: OpenDRIVE carries only static road-network content (geometry, lanes, signals, objects). Vehicles, routes and trajectories belong to OpenSCENARIO; fine surface texture/roughness (potholes, cobbles) belongs to OpenCRG and is only referenced from OpenDRIVE.
right: Emit static network only: roads, lanes, junctions, signals, static objects
Represent detailed surface roughness only via <surface><CRG> references, if at all
wrong: Encoding traffic flow, routes or vehicles in OpenDRIVE - that is OpenSCENARIO content
Modelling potholes or paving texture with elevation/shape polynomials - surface detail is OpenCRG's job

section: 5.1 User Data / 5.2 Including Data / 5.4 Description of the data quality (Core UML)
caption: Figure 4. UML model ASAM OpenDRIVE Core
shows: UML 'class Core'. t_OpenDRIVE (orange) has: +header (no multiplicity = exactly 1) t_header, +road 1..* Road::t_road, +controller 0..* Signal::t_controller, +junction 0..* Junction::t_junction, +junctionGroup 0..* Junction::t_junctionGroup, +station 0..* Railroad::t_station (blue = other packages). All generalise (hollow triangle) to abstract _OpenDriveElement, which has g_additionalData 0..* (t_OpenDRIVE also links to it 0..*). g_additionalData groups +userData 0..* t_userData (code: string mandatory, value: string [0..1], 0..* userDataContent), +include 0..* t_include (file: string), +dataQuality 0..1 t_dataQuality. t_dataQuality has +error 0..1 t_dataQuality_Error (xyAbsolute, xyRelative, zAbsolute, zRelative: double, all mandatory) and +rawData 0..1 t_dataQuality_RawData (date: string, postProcessing: enum, source: enum mandatory; postProcessingComment, sourceComment [0..1]). Separate primitive types t_zeroOne, t_grEqZero, t_grZero, all specialisations of double.
lesson: A valid file needs exactly one header and at least one road; junctions/controllers are optional. Any element (not only the root) may carry userData/include/dataQuality, so provenance (e.g. the OSM way id) can be attached per road/lane/object. If <error> is written, all four error values are mandatory. t_grZero = strictly > 0, t_grEqZero = >= 0, t_zeroOne = [0,1].
right: Always emit one <header> and at least one <road>
Attach OSM provenance as <userData code="osm_way_id" value="..."/> on the element it describes
If writing <dataQuality><error>, provide xyAbsolute, xyRelative, zAbsolute and zRelative together
In <rawData> always give date, source and postProcessing; name OpenStreetMap in sourceComment
wrong: Producing a file with zero roads (violates road 1..*)
Writing only xyAbsolute in <error> - the other three are mandatory
Assuming userData is only allowed at file level
Treating t_grZero fields (e.g. geometry length) as allowing 0

caption: Figure 5. Available coordinate systems in ASAM OpenDRIVE
shows: Three identical right-handed axis triads side by side: Inertial System (x blue forward-right, y green to the left, z red up), Reference Line System (s forward, t left, h up), Local System (u forward, v left, z up).
lesson: All three systems share the same handedness and layout: the second axis (y, t, v) points LEFT of the first, the third points up. +t / +v is left of the direction of s / u, and positive rotations are counter-clockwise seen from above.
right: Left normal for +t: n = (-sin hdg, cos hdg)
Treat s->t->h exactly like x->y->z (right-handed)
wrong: Using a screen convention with y down, or t pointing right - mirrors every lane
Feeding a left-handed engine convention (e.g. Unreal/CARLA with y to the right) without converting - flips t, headings and curvature signs
formula: t-unit = (-sin(hdg), cos(hdg)); h = s x t

caption: Figure 6. Coordinate systems in ASAM OpenDRIVE interacting with another
shows: Inertial X/Y grid with a blue reference line curving to the upper right. At a point labelled 'reference line system' s is tangent to the line and t perpendicular pointing up-left. A grey segment leads down-right to a 'local system' point, with a right-angle mark between this segment and the tangent; at the local origin u points down-right and v up-right, i.e. the local frame is rotated relative to s/t.
lesson: A local origin is found by going to s on the reference line and then moving perpendicular to the tangent by t (here t < 0, i.e. to the right). The local axes may additionally carry their own heading relative to s/t.
right: Place objects/signals at P = refline(s) + t * leftNormal(s)
Apply an object's heading on top of the reference-line heading at s
wrong: Offsetting t along the inertial y-axis instead of perpendicular to the tangent
Assuming the local u axis is aligned with s - only true when the local heading is 0
formula: P(s,t) = (x(s) - t*sin(hdg(s)), y(s) + t*cos(hdg(s)))

caption: Figure 7. Inertial coordinate system with defined rotations
shows: Three-step rotation sequence. Panel 1 'heading > 0': rotation about z (z = z'), x turns counter-clockwise to x', y to y'. Panel 2 'heading = 0, pitch > 0': rotation about y' (y' = y''); x'' is drawn BELOW x' (tips down) and z'' leans toward the former x direction. Panel 3 'heading = 0, pitch = 0, roll > 0': rotation about x'' (x'' = x'''); y''' is lifted ABOVE y'' and z''' leans away from y (toward the right).
lesson: Rotation order is heading (about z), then pitch (about the new y'), then roll (about the new x''). All angles follow the right-hand rule: positive heading = counter-clockwise from above; positive pitch = nose DOWN (x tips toward -z); positive roll = left side (+y) UP, right side down.
right: Build R = Rz(heading) * Ry(pitch) * Rx(roll) (intrinsic z, y', x'')
An object whose front points uphill has NEGATIVE pitch
An object banked with its left side higher has positive roll
wrong: Using the aviation/graphics habit 'positive pitch = nose up' - inverts every slope
Applying roll before pitch/heading, or using extrinsic rotations
Treating heading as a compass bearing (north = 0, clockwise) instead of a CCW angle from +x (east)
formula: R = Rz(h)*Ry(p)*Rx(r); pitch=+pi/2 -> x'' = -z; roll=+pi/2 -> z''' = -y''

caption: Figure 8. Inertial coordinate system with defined rotations
shows: Four box sketches seen from the front (x toward the viewer, y left, z up). (a) all angles 0: only y and z visible. (b) heading < 0: x' appears pointing to the viewer's right and a side face becomes visible, z' = z. (c) heading < 0, pitch < 0: the box tilts so its top face is visible; x'' points right and upward, y'' = y'. (d) heading < 0, pitch < 0, roll > 0: additionally rolled - z''' leans right and the left (y''') edge is raised, x''' = x''.
lesson: Same convention as Figure 7, demonstrated with negative angles: negative heading = clockwise from above (x turns toward -y); negative pitch = front lifts up; positive roll = +y side up.
right: Use negative heading for a clockwise yaw from +x
Use negative pitch for an object whose front points upward
wrong: Reading pitch < 0 as nose down - it is nose up
Interpreting heading < 0 as turning left

caption: Figure 9. Reference line coordinate system
shows: Inertial X/Y grid (x = 1..7, y = 1..6) with an S-shaped grey road. A dashed reference line runs down its middle with labels s = 0 .. s = 8 at equal spacing along the line; dashed cross-lines at each tick run perpendicular to the line across the road. At s = 0 (about x = 2.2, y = 1.2) a blue s arrow points along the line and a green t arrow perpendicular to its left. Between neighbouring ticks the outer edge of each bend is visibly longer than the inner edge.
lesson: s is arc length ALONG the reference line (in the xy-plane), starting at 0 at the road start; t is measured perpendicular to the local tangent, positive left. Because cross-sections are perpendicular to the reference line, equal ds maps to unequal lengths on lane borders (longer outside a bend, shorter inside).
right: Parameterise lanes, objects and signals by reference-line arc length s starting at 0 for each road
Compute lane-border lengths separately when needed (e.g. marking dash spacing) - they differ from ds
Keep |t * curvature| < 1 so cross-sections do not cross on the inside of bends
wrong: Using chord length or straight OSM node-to-node distances as s on curved geometry
Continuing s from the previous road (s restarts at 0 for every road)
Applying lane widths along x or y instead of along the normal
formula: offset-curve length element: dl = (1 - t*kappa(s)) ds

caption: Figure 10. Reference line system with defined rotations
shows: Two panels. Left: heading rotation about h (h = h'); s turns counter-clockwise to s', t to t'. Right: roll about s (s = s'''); t''' lifted above t, h''' leans away from t (to the right). No pitch panel exists.
lesson: The reference-line frame has only two rotational degrees of freedom: heading (from planView geometry) and roll (from superelevation). There is no pitch - elevation lifts the frame vertically without tilting s.
right: Derive the s/t/h frame from planView heading and superelevation roll only
Positive superelevation = left (+t) side up
wrong: Pitching the s-axis with the elevation gradient when computing t-offsets or lane widths
Treating superelevation as positive when the right side is raised

caption: Figure 11. Heading in reference line
shows: Inertial X/Y grid with a grey reference line rising to the right. At its start s points slightly up-right and t up-left; at a later point s' and t' are rotated more steeply, following the tangent. Text in the frame: 'Heading caused by <geometry>'.
lesson: The reference-line heading at any s comes solely from planView geometry (start hdg of the containing geometry plus accumulated curvature) and varies continuously along curved geometry.
right: Evaluate heading at s from the containing <geometry> (hdg + integral of curvature)
Ensure heading continuity at geometry boundaries
wrong: Using a single heading per road
Taking heading from raw OSM segment directions without smoothing (kinks)
formula: hdg(s) = hdg0 + integral from s0 to s of kappa(u) du

caption: Figure 12. Roll in reference line
shows: Cross-section of the road seen looking along +s (s is the blue dot at height 0 on an axis labelled 'Z'; the horizontal axis is labelled 'X'). A thick road line passes through s, higher on the LEFT where the green t arrow points and lower on the right. An arc marks the roll angle between the horizontal and the road line; the dashed vertical h is rotated to h', which leans right. Text: 'Roll caused by <superelevation>'.
lesson: Superelevation is a roll of the s/t/h frame about s; positive roll raises the left (+t) side and tilts h toward -t. The pivot is the reference line (t = 0): points with t > 0 rise and t < 0 drop by t*tan(roll).
right: Lateral height: z = z_ref(s) + t*tan(superelevation(s)) (plus lateral shape)
A right-hand curve (negative curvature) is banked left-side-high, i.e. positive superelevation
wrong: Pivoting the bank around the road edge instead of the reference line
Sign error: raising the right side for positive superelevation
Reading the horizontal 'X' label literally - the section lies in the t-h plane, with t to the left
formula: dz(t) = t * tan(roll(s))

caption: Figure 13. Elevation in reference line
shows: Side view: vertical z axis with 0 marked; a grey elevation curve is flat at z = 0, rises smoothly, then levels off. Two s/t/h frames are drawn, one at z = 0 and one on the rising part; in BOTH s is horizontal and h vertical - the frame is translated up, not tilted. Text: '<elevation> projected on reference line'.
lesson: Elevation only shifts the reference-line frame vertically; the frame is never pitched, and s remains the horizontal (xy-projected) arc length. A 10 % grade over 100 m of s still has s-length 100 m, not 100.5 m.
right: Compute s and geometry @length purely in 2D
Evaluate z(s) from the elevation polynomial and translate (never rotate) the s/t frame
wrong: Using 3D arc length (including climb) as s or as geometry length
Pitching lanes/objects with the slope when computing lateral positions
Fitting elevation polynomials against 3D distance instead of planar s
formula: z(s) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3 with ds = s - s_start; s measured in the xy-plane

caption: Figure 14. Local system with defined rotations
shows: Same three-panel rotation drawing as Figure 7 with u/v/z: heading about z (u -> u' counter-clockwise), pitch about v (v = v''; u'' tips down, z'' leans forward), roll about u (u = u'''; v''' lifted, z''' leans right).
lesson: The local (object) frame uses the identical heading-pitch-roll convention as the inertial frame: heading CCW positive about z, positive pitch = front (u) down, positive roll = left (v) side up, applied in the order heading, pitch, roll.
right: Reuse the same rotation code for local and inertial frames
wrong: Using different sign conventions for object orientation than for the inertial system
formula: R_local = Rz(heading)*Ry(pitch)*Rx(roll)

caption: Figure 15. Local coordinate systems with heading, pitch, roll
shows: Four box sketches identical to Figure 8 but labelled u/v/z: all zero; heading < 0 (u' to the viewer's right); heading < 0 and pitch < 0 (top face visible, u'' pointing right and up, v'' = v'); plus roll > 0 (left edge raised, u''' = u'').
lesson: Confirms local angle signs match the inertial convention: negative heading = clockwise, negative pitch lifts the front, positive roll lifts the left side.
right: Same sign handling as Figure 8 for objects placed in local coordinates
wrong: Interpreting a local heading as a compass bearing

caption: Figure 16. Local coordinate system with respect to reference line system
shows: Inertial grid with blue reference line; reference-line system at a point with s along the tangent and t up-left (right angle marked). A local origin lies below-right of it (t < 0). At the local origin an unrotated pair u (parallel to s) / v (parallel to t, solid green) is drawn plus a rotated pair u'/v' (dashed) turned counter-clockwise, with an arrow marking the angle from u to u'. Text: 'Heading of local coordinate system with respect to reference line coordinate system'.
lesson: An object's local heading is measured relative to the reference-line tangent at its s, not relative to inertial east. Heading 0 means the object faces +s; the unrotated local frame is parallel to s/t at the projected point.
right: Inertial yaw of an object = hdg_refline(s) + object.hdg
Express orientation of OSM point features relative to the road tangent
wrong: Writing an absolute (inertial or compass) yaw into object @hdg - wrong on any road not running due east
Trusting the phrase '0.0 = east' in the 6.4 text - the figure shows the heading is relative to s
formula: yaw_inertial = hdg_ref(s) + hdg_local

section: 6.5 Summary of all available coordinate systems
caption: Figure 17. Summary of coordinate system in ASAM OpenDRIVE
shows: Perspective sketch: inertial system at lower left (x, y, z); a blue reference line with a reference-line system at one point (s tangent, t left, h up); dashed lines project that point onto the inertial x and y directions; a local system (u, v, z) beside the reference line, linked to the reference point by dashed lines and slightly rotated relative to s/t.
lesson: The systems are chained: inertial -> reference line (via geometry x, y, hdg plus elevation/superelevation at s) -> local (via s, t, zOffset and local heading/pitch/roll). Local placements are never given directly in inertial coordinates.
right: Implement local->s/t/h->x/y/z as a composition of two transforms
Convert OSM point features to (s, t) by projecting onto the nearest road reference line
wrong: Writing inertial x/y directly into s/t attributes
Ignoring reference-line elevation/roll when converting local z to inertial z
formula: X_obj = X_ref(s) + R_ref(s)*([0, t, 0] + R_local*p_local)

caption: Figure 18. geoReference and offset
shows: Inertial X/Y plot with broken axes. Lower left: an S-shaped road in 'OpenDRIVE x/y coordinates' (x about 10-45, y about 10-35), its start marked with a red circle near (15, 10) and small s/t arrows. Upper right: the identical, unrotated road in 'Geo referenced x/y coordinates' (x about 500000-500030, y about 40005-40030), start also circled. Brackets 'x offset' and 'y offset' span the distance between the two start points.
lesson: The header <offset> is a translation from small, numerically safe OpenDRIVE coordinates to projected map coordinates (e.g. UTM easting incl. its 500000 m false easting): projected = OpenDRIVE + offset. The figure shows no rotation, consistent with the rule that @hdg should be avoided.
right: Store geometry near (0,0) and write <offset x=E0 y=N0 z=Z0 hdg="0"/> in the header
Keep <geoReference> as the unmodified EPSG/PROJ string (with its own +x_0/+y_0)
Recover map coordinates as E = x + offset.x, N = y + offset.y
wrong: Writing raw UTM coordinates (~5e5, ~5e6) into geometry @x/@y (precision loss; against the rule)
Folding the offset into the proj string by editing +x_0/+y_0
Subtracting the offset when converting to map coordinates (sign inversion)
Using a non-zero offset @hdg
formula: x_geo = x_odr + offset.x; y_geo = y_odr + offset.y (with hdg = 0)

caption: Figure 19. Geometry elements in ASAM OpenDRIVE
shows: Five matplotlib thumbnails: 'straight lines' (line from (0,0) to (5,1.25)), 'spirals' (clothoid curling inward), 'arcs' (arc rising and flattening), 'cubic polynomials' (y(x) cubic with a local wiggle on x in [-4,4]), 'Parametric cubic polynomials' (curve bending gently down from 0 to about -0.6 over about 60 m).
lesson: Exactly five planView primitives exist: line, spiral, arc, poly3 (deprecated) and paramPoly3. Prefer line/arc/spiral (exact, curvature-continuous) or paramPoly3 for free-form fits.
right: Emit line/spiral/arc for designed shapes and paramPoly3 for smoothed measured polylines
wrong: Emitting new poly3 geometry (deprecated in 1.7)
Approximating curves with many tiny lines (curvature jumps and heading kinks)

caption: Figure 20. The individual parts of a road
shows: Top row: 'reference line' + 'lanes' + 'features' = composite road. Bottom: perspective view of a two-lane road; the blue reference line runs between a yellow lane labelled '1' (left) and a blue lane labelled '-1' (right). Arrows at the bottom: s along the reference line away from the viewer, t pointing left. Speed-limit signs '60' (far) and '80' (near) stand on the right roadside.
lesson: A road is three layers: reference line (geometry), lanes defined relative to it, and features (signals/objects) placed in s/t. Lanes left of the reference line (+t) have positive IDs, right lanes negative IDs; the reference line is the zero-width centre lane 0 between them.
right: Put the reference line on the boundary between left and right lanes for two-way roads
Number lanes 1, 2, ... outward on the left and -1, -2, ... outward on the right
Place right-roadside signals with t < 0
wrong: Giving right-side lanes positive IDs
Assuming the reference-line direction implies driving direction (the text says it does not)

caption: Figure 21. UML model Road Geometry including the Reference Line elements
shows: UML 'class RoadGeometry'. t_road_planView has +geometry 1..* t_road_planView_geometry (hdg: double, length: t_grZero, s: t_grEqZero, x: double, y: double) with children +line (no attributes), +spiral (curvEnd, curvStart: double), +arc (curvature: double), +poly3 (a, b, c, d), +paramPoly3 (aU, aV, bU, bV, cU, cV, dU, dV: double, pRange: e_paramPoly3_pRange - no [0..1], i.e. mandatory). t_road_lateralProfile has +superelevation 0..* (a, b, c, d, s: t_grEqZero) and +shape 0..* (a, b, c, d, s, t). t_road_elevationProfile has +elevation 0..* (a, b, c, d, s). t_road_surface has +CRG 0..* (file, mode, orientation, sStart, sEnd mandatory; hOffset, purpose, sOffset, tOffset, zOffset, zScale optional).
lesson: Every planView needs at least one geometry; geometry length must be strictly > 0 (t_grZero), s >= 0. paramPoly3 must always carry pRange. Elevation, superelevation and shape records are optional.
right: Drop or merge zero-length segments before writing geometry
Always write pRange="arcLength" or "normalized" on paramPoly3
Write geometry records in ascending s, starting at 0
wrong: Emitting <geometry length="0"> for degenerate OSM segments
Omitting pRange and relying on a reader default
Writing two primitives inside one <geometry>

caption: Figure 22. A straight line
shows: matplotlib plot of one straight segment from about (-47, 1) to about (-1.7, 35.7) m; axes 'x-axis [m]', 'y-axis [m]'. It matches the XML example: x = -47.17, y = 0.728, hdg = 0.6548 rad, length = 57.28 (end = (-1.6, 35.4)).
lesson: A line is fully defined by start (x, y), hdg and length; the end point follows. hdg is the mathematical angle from +x (0.655 rad ~ 37.5 deg, north-east).
right: End = start + length*(cos hdg, sin hdg)
Use that end as the next geometry's start (no leaps)
wrong: Storing end coordinates instead of length
Writing hdg in degrees
formula: x(ds) = x0 + ds*cos(hdg); y(ds) = y0 + ds*sin(hdg)

caption: Figure 23. Road geometry described by a spiral
shows: matplotlib plot (sub-metre scale) of a clothoid starting at (0, 0) heading straight up (+y) with zero curvature, bending right (clockwise) with ever-increasing curvature over the top near (0.43, 0.78), down past (0.72, 0.5) and curling inward to end near (0.34, 0.49) - more than a full turn. Not drawn from the XML example values.
lesson: A spiral's curvature changes linearly with arc length; as |curvature| grows it winds into an ever-tighter curl. Clockwise winding = negative curvature (right curve). Position requires Fresnel-type integration; an arc approximation is wrong.
right: kappa(ds) = curvStart + (curvEnd - curvStart)*ds/length
Evaluate via Fresnel integrals or accurate numeric integration
Use negative curvature values for right-hand transitions
wrong: Approximating a spiral by an arc with average curvature
Assuming spirals must start or end at curvature 0
Writing curvStart = curvEnd (rule: should differ - use an arc)
formula: kappa(ds) = cS + (cE - cS)*ds/L; hdg(ds) = hdg0 + cS*ds + (cE - cS)*ds^2/(2L); x = x0 + int cos(hdg) ds; y = y0 + int sin(hdg) ds

caption: Figure 24. Road geometry described by an arc
shows: matplotlib plot of an arc starting near (0, 72) heading east (+x) and bending clockwise down to about (70.5, 12.5); radius about 71-72 m with the centre near the origin (a single dot is plotted at (0, 0)); sweep about 80 deg. Not drawn from the XML example (example curvature -0.127 1/m).
lesson: An arc has constant curvature = 1/R; a clockwise (right-turning) arc has negative curvature and its centre lies on the -t (right) side at distance R from the start.
right: curvature = -1/R for right curves, +1/R for left curves
Centre = start + (1/kappa)*(-sin hdg, cos hdg)
wrong: Writing positive curvature for a clockwise arc
Writing curvature 0 (use <line>)
Writing radius instead of curvature
formula: x = x0 + (sin(hdg0 + k*ds) - sin(hdg0))/k; y = y0 - (cos(hdg0 + k*ds) - cos(hdg0))/k

section: 7.5 Generating arbitrary road courses from geometry elements
caption: Figure 25. Creating a reference line from geometry elements
shows: Left: five colour-coded pieces in order - line (orange), spiral (blue), arc (green), spiral (blue), arc (green). Right: they are chained into one smooth reference line bending left toward the upper right, with s/t frames at start (t up-left) and end (s pointing up, t pointing left). Bottom: curvature-vs-s plot - 0 along the line, linear ramp up (spiral), constant (arc), linear ramp DOWN to a smaller but still positive value (spiral), constant (arc); steering-wheel icons show straight, turning left, held, partly unwound, held.
lesson: Geometry elements are concatenated so that position, heading AND curvature are continuous; spirals play the role of turning the steering wheel between different curvatures, including arc-to-arc transitions between two non-zero curvatures. Positive curvature = left turn.
right: Insert spirals between line and arc and between arcs of different radius
Check position, heading and curvature continuity at every geometry join
Use spirals with non-zero curvStart and curvEnd for compound curves
wrong: Line directly followed by arc (curvature jump - allowed but not recommended)
Assuming spiral curvature always returns to zero
Heading mismatch at joins producing kinks
formula: kappa(s) piecewise linear and continuous

caption: Figure 26. A cubic polynom
shows: matplotlib plot of y(x) for x in [-100, 100] m: starts at y = -75, flattens to a plateau near y = 20 around x = 0, climbs to y = 125 at x = 100. Coefficients a = 20, b = 0, c = 0.0005, d = 0.0001.
lesson: A plain cubic in inertial x/y is a function y(x): one y per x. This is only background; <poly3> is evaluated in a local u/v frame.
wrong: Evaluating <poly3> coefficients against inertial x instead of local u
formula: y(x) = a + b*x + c*x^2 + d*x^3

caption: Figure 27. A curve which cannot be represented by a cubic polynom w.r.t x parameter
shows: Inertial X/Y grid with a curve from (3, 1.5) rising and bending back over itself near x = 5; a vertical red line at x ~ 4.85 hits the curve twice (y ~ 3.3 and y ~ 4.3). Warning icon and text 'two Y-values for one X-value'.
lesson: A curve that turns back in x cannot be written as y(x); poly3 must be expressed in a rotated local frame where it is a single-valued function of u, so u must increase monotonically along the curve.
right: Choose the local u axis along the start heading so v(u) is single-valued
Use paramPoly3 when the heading changes by ~90 deg or more relative to the start
wrong: Fitting poly3 in global x
